***

# The Triumph of the Doomed: Joy in the Face of Mortality

Across the rolling canvas of the countryside, a column of soldiers marches toward the front lines. Their voices rise in vibrant, unified song, creating a striking paradox: men moving briskly toward their probable destruction, yet filling the air with melodies of joy. Rather than marching in the solemn silence of dread, they traverse the landscape with an exuberant spirit, confronting the grim reality of battle not with tears, but with triumphant music.

This unyielding cheerfulness forms the moral heart of the poem, which serves as a passionate exhortation to the condemned. The speaker urges the soldiers to cast away all lingering regret, sorrow, and longing for what might have been. Instead of viewing their fatal destination as a tragedy to be resisted, they are called to embrace it with open-hearted gladness. In doing so, they transcend the role of mere victims of war; by willingly accepting their fate, they transform a march to slaughter into a triumphant act of human spirit.

To soften the terror of this end, the poem offers a timeless, cosmic perspective on human mortality. The Earth itself regards death without fear or grief. It is an impartial custodian that receives the fallen soldier with the very same indifferent grace it extended to the greatest figures in human history. Whether it be the hemlock-poisoned philosopher Socrates or Jesus Christ upon the cross, the earth opens to take back all life equally. In the grand tapestry of existence, the death of a soldier is neither a anomaly nor a ruinous defeat, but a natural returning home.

Moreover, the natural world acts as an enduring vessel for the soldiers’ spirit. Long after the artillery falls silent and the men’s physical voices are forever stilled by death, the surrounding landscape will not forget them. The hills, winds, and fields will absorb their melodies, storing and echoing their songs across generations. Their mortal bodies may decay, but the joyful energy they released into the open air will linger as a permanent whisper in the natural world.

Ultimately, the poem culminates in a powerful call to arms—not for battle, but for the peaceful surrender to the inevitable. The soldiers are urged to march merrily straight into the very gates of death. By planting their joy deep into the soil of their final battlefield, they sow the seeds of their own eternal rest. In exchanging their fleeting worldly anxieties for the quiet embrace of the earth, they earn a deep, undisturbed peace, knowing that their final act was one of beauty, courage, and unshakeable joy.

Here is an expansion of the summary into a complete poem:

***

**The Song of the Marching**

The heavy tread of iron-shod boots resounds,
A steady line beneath a darkening sky.
No armor shields them from the fate ahead;
They tread the road where mortal men must die.

Yet shed the heavy mantle of regret,
Unclench the hand that clings to yesterday.
Forget the quiet hearths, the unplowed fields,
And cast the bitter weight of grief away.

Raise up your throats and let a song break forth!
Fill all the hollow air with wild delight;
March to the red horizon not in woe,
But sing your gladness out against the night.

For far below, the ancient earth attends,
Ready to catch each vibrant, ringing note.
The patient soil will drink your joy complete,
Absorbing all the praise your music spoke.

And when the battle fades and silence falls,
When every mortal cadence comes to rest,
Your song will slumber in the deep-dug clay,
Enfolded safely in the valley’s breast.

Through root and stone, through spring's returning green,
That gladness shall endure, renewed and brave—
A stoic anthem woven in the dust,
A quiet triumph rising from the grave.

***

All the hills and vales along
Earth is giving song,
Blown across the scanning sea,
On to wind and waves and me.
By the roadside, on the steep,
It awakens folks from sleep,
Giving them a morning cheer,
Making old things bright and clear.
    Earth that gave the man his birth,
    Gives him back his ancient earth,
    Earth that made him, takes him home.
    Earth, the mother of the foam,
    Earth, the lover of the rain,
    Takes her children back again.

On, march on, the music cries,
For the morning breaks and dies,
And the sun has done his best
To set bright into the west.
March, my brothers, march away,
Youth is short and dies today.
    Earth that gave the man his birth,
    Gives him back his ancient earth,
    Earth that made him, takes him home.
    Earth, the mother of the foam,
    Earth, the lover of the rain,
    Takes her children back again.

Ill it suits you, helpless ones,
To be fawning on the suns,
Or to weep for shadows cast
By the tall trees moving past.
Up and away, the song is done,
Sing, ye soldier-men, sing on!
    Earth that gave the man his birth,
    Gives him back his ancient earth,
    Earth that made him, takes him home.
    Earth, the mother of the foam,
    Earth, the lover of the rain,
    Takes her children back again.

Pour your light along the way,
Sing your song while yet 'tis day,
Ere the night come down and wrap you,
And the quiet earth entrap you.
Yield your strength, nor ask a reason,
Earth will have you in due season.
    Earth that gave the man his birth,
    Gives him back his ancient earth,
    Earth that made him, takes him home.
    Earth, the mother of the foam,
    Earth, the lover of the rain,
    Takes her children back again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of a World War I soldier-poet about marching men heading cheerfully toward their own deaths, drawing parallels to Socrates and Christ.
counterfactuals.output:
We march with whistles through the falling mire,
Young faces flushed beneath the weight of lead,
Approaching joyful to the wall of fire,
As though the earth were made to house the dead.
A chorus rises from the muddy line,
A music sweet, though tuned to meet the grave;
They drink the rain as if it were the wine,
And laugh to think how little they can save.

Like him who raised the Athenian bitter bowl
And drank the hemlock with a quiet grace,
Each lad accepts the poison in his soul
And wears a calm philosophy of face.
No curse they utter for the council’s lie,
No bitter tears for truth so soon betrayed;
They take the hemlock from the slate-gray sky,
And drink the dark, untroubled, unafraid.

And like the Man who bore the heavy tree
Up the red slope of ruin, raw and wide,
They shoulder crosses toward their Calvary,
With iron bayonets slung against their side.
Their packs are heavy, and the barbed wire weaves
A crown of thorns across the shattered hill;
Yet through the smoke, no soldier cowers or grieves—
They bless the hands that march them out to kill.

How light they step! As if the hemlock’s draught
Were honeyed nectar from a summer plain;
As if the nails that wait them were a craft
To stitch their names above the touch of pain.
They break their youth like bread for all to share,
And pour their blood upon the sodden sod,
Unknowing priests who offer up a prayer,
And smile their way into the mouth of God.

Forgive them, Lord, the laughter in their breath,
The song that rings across the iron wire;
For like the wise and holy in their death,
They walk serenely through the slaughter-fire.
Magnificently young, and blind, and true,
They know not—or know well—just what they do.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: What is the text of the poem that begins with "All the hills and vales along Earth is bursting into song"?
counterfactuals.output:
This is the poem **"All the Hills and Vales Along"** by the Scottish World War I poet **Charles Hamilton Sorley** (1895–1915). He wrote it in 1915, shortly before he was killed in action at the Battle of Loos at the age of 20. 

Here is the complete text of the poem:

***

**All the Hills and Vales Along**
*by Charles Hamilton Sorley*

All the hills and vales along
Earth is bursting into song,
And the valley echoing all
Spurns them back its chant royal.
Because you are going out to die,
Cry glad words at the earth and sky.
Not that you may be remembered,
Not that you may be revered,
Not that your name may be cheered,
Not that your memories may be endeared,
For the earth is very old,
And the earth has lost its hold
Of the countless names of old,
Names of men who died for her.
Give your lives, but do not stir
Your soul to any hope of fame:
You shall pass, but not your name.

On, marching men, on
To the gates of death, along!
Pour your life out empty, go,
Singing loud and laughing low,
Grave the sky with your brave song,
Grave the sky with your brave song!

Earth that breathed the breath of life
Urges you to join the strife.
Earth that retains the dead
Urges you to shed
Your blood upon her lap, so that
Fertile, rich, and free may be
The earth that gave you life.
Charges you to give again
That which she gave you, and in vain
Gave you, if you refuse to die.

On, marching men, on
To the gates of death, along!
Pour your life out empty, go,
Singing loud and laughing low,
Grave the sky with your brave song,
Grave the sky with your brave song!

Earth that takes the lives of men
Gives them back their strength again,
Gives them back their beauty, gives
Everything that lives.
They shall pass, but not the earth.
They shall die, but not the birth.
So they go, with singing heart,
To their part.

On, marching men, on
To the gates of death, along!
Pour your life out empty, go,
Singing loud and laughing low,
Grave the sky with your brave song,
Grave the sky with your brave song!

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you provide a famous British anti-war poem from 1915 that uses a rhythmic, rhyming meter to describe soldiers marching to the front line?
counterfactuals.output:
A prominent poem that matches your description is **"All the Hills and Vales Along"** by the Scottish-British poet **Charles Hamilton Sorley**, written in **1915**. 

Sorley wrote this poem shortly before he was killed in action at the Battle of Loos in October 1915 at the age of 20. 

The poem uses a driving, rhythmic, marching meter (trochaic tetrameter) that mimics the heavy, synchronized sound of soldiers' boots. Beneath its deceptively energetic cadence lies a dark, ironic anti-war message: the soldiers march cheerfully toward their own doom, while nature remains indifferent to their sacrifice.

---

### **"All the Hills and Vales Along"**
*by Charles Hamilton Sorley (1915)*

All the hills and vales along
Earth is bursting into song,
Which the weary march along
With a sound of shouting!
As they march dead men to be,
Their eyes are proper light to see,
Their mouths are proper gifts for use
For noble ends, or so they choose,
Or rhyme and run, or jest and chat,
It does not matter much for that:
Soon they will be down and put
Underneath the soldier’s boot.

Earth that leaned and listened long
To the call of seed and song,
Sits and waits that she may lose
The double terror of her shoes:
Earth that holds them down to-day
Will release them to-morrow to play
In the light of the sun and the rain.
Earth who took back all again
Which she gave, will give again
Freely to the sun and rain.

On, march on, feel no dismay,
Earth’s a thief who steals away,
Which she will give back again
Freely to the sun and rain.
Earth will match your soldier's boots
To the rhythm of the roots.
Earth will bring you all to dust,
Take your body, as she must:
Earth will wrap you in her fold,
Give you quiet, make you cold.

On, march on, feel no dismay,
More than even the day's total.
Earth is eager to cover up
The heavy blood, the broken cup.
Pour the wine and drain the bowl,
Give your dust to the earth’s control.
Earth will wrap you in her fold,
Give you quiet, make you cold.
Earth that leaned and listened long
To the call of seed and song,
Will release you into song!

---

### **Why it fits your request:**
* **Written in 1915:** Written by Sorley in May 1915 while serving on the Western Front.
* **Rhythmic, Rhyming Meter:** It employs a strong, driving beat that mimics a military marching song or drumbeat.
* **Content:** It depicts troops marching out to the front line while explicitly reminding the reader that these young men are "marching dead men to be." 
* **Anti-War Tone:** Unlike the jingoistic propoganda of early WWI, Sorley strips away the romance of war, presenting death not as a heroic victory, but as a quick return to cold dust.
